name: breadth stated as a positive capability of UTF-8 vs breadth mentioned only as a hazard of accepting non-ASCII bytes
side_a: Credit when the answer attributes the wider coverage to UTF-8 as a property/advantage of the encoding itself — i.e., it says UTF-8 can represent/handle a broader range of characters (ideally noting it is a superset of / backwards compatible with ASCII). Do not deduct merely because the answer also adds caveats.
side_b: Deduct when the only comparative remark is framed as a danger of UTF-8 permitting illegal/unexpected input (e.g., 'more permissive', 'could allow invalid characters', 'could allow non-ASCII data to pass through'), i.e. the answer characterizes what UTF-8 would *admit* in this header rather than asserting the encoding's larger character repertoire. Such risk-framing is not a breadth claim and earns no point.

name: Endorses UTF-8 as the better default vs defends keeping ASCII
side_a: No_deduct if the answer actually agrees that UTF-8 should (generally) replace ASCII as the default decoding for the host, i.e., it affirms the proposed change and explains that UTF-8 is ASCII-backwards-compatible and avoids the decode failure.
side_b: Deduct if the answer rejects the change and argues ASCII should be kept (appealing to RFC/Punycode strictness, 'fail fast', 'catch protocol violations', security), since it never concedes the point the item is asking for.
